claims.claim: For m,n≥2, the sortable component has Q=(mn)! states if m or n is even and Q=(mn)!/2 states if both are odd.
claims.evidence: A row push is an n-cycle and a column push an m-cycle. When both dimensions are odd all generators are even; the source characterization supplies the converse that every even configuration is reachable. If either dimension is even, the same characterization gives all permutations. The component therefore has the stated cardinality.
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Direct parity and component-size proof from the source characterization.

claims.claim: On a p×q board where pushes in both directions are allowed, an involution π on any chosen row can be applied in at most 3q+3a₂(π) pushes, with the only side effect being a one-step cyclic shift, in a chosen direction, of the body of each of a₂(π) fixed auxiliary columns.
claims.evidence: In the source's standing p,q≥2 regime, each of the three scans uses q row pushes and one push of each of k=a₂(π) auxiliary columns once inverse pushes are allowed directly. Thus the exact cost is 3q+3k. The source position trace then gives precisely the requested row transpositions and one cyclic body shift on each fixed auxiliary column, with every other position fixed.
claims.witness: The exact checker verified 4,720 constructions for 2≤p,q≤6, every chosen row, every involution, and both side-effect directions.
claims.search_method: Symbolic position-permutation construction plus exhaustive finite checks.

claims.claim: Every even permutation is a product συ of two involutions with a₂(σ)=a₂(υ); every odd permutation is a product συτ where τ is a transposition and a₂(σ)=a₂(υ).
claims.evidence: Odd-length cycles admit two reflection factors with equal transposition counts. Each even-length cycle admits either sign of a one-transposition imbalance. An even permutation has an even number of even-length cycles, so the imbalances pair; for an odd permutation, one remaining transposition can be split from the larger last factor. Disjoint-cycle factors combine into involutions.
claims.witness: All 5,913 permutations on at most seven symbols were checked for the required factorization.
claims.search_method: Cycle-reflection proof and exhaustive exact enumeration.

claims.claim: For arbitrary p,q≥2, FillColumns makes every column near-full using O(pq log q) pushes; the proof does not require p≤q.
claims.evidence: Each column is pushed at most p−1 times. With Ψ equal to the number of incorrectly colored body tokens, a complete q-push scan decreases Ψ by at least half the current number f of underfull columns. In a dyadic f-phase, Ψ≤(p−1)f yields O(p) complete scans, hence O(pq) row pushes per phase and O(pq log q) overall. No step uses p≤q.
claims.witness: Exhaustive executions covered all 2×2, 2×3, and 3×2 configurations, with additional 4×2, 2×4, and 3×3 cases.
claims.search_method: Potential-function proof and direct algorithm simulation in both aspect-ratio orientations.

claims.claim: For arbitrary p,q≥2, FloatMinimums transforms a matrix whose columns are all near-full into one whose columns are all body-full using O(pq) pushes.
claims.evidence: Near-fullness leaves exactly one token of each target-column class among the heads. A q-step head-row sweep aligns each such token with its class column. At alignment, at most p−1 column pushes place that column's unique target-row-one token at its head, after which the column is not touched. The cost is at most q+q(p−1)=pq and each resulting body has exactly its target set.
claims.witness: The exact FillColumns/FloatMinimums simulations all ended body-full within the stated push bound.
claims.search_method: Token-count argument and exact state simulation.

claims.claim: Given a p×q matrix in which every column is body-full, its buffer row can be sorted in O(q) bidirectional pushes while preserving the set of tokens in every column body.
claims.evidence: The heads are exactly the q buffer tokens. For an even head correction, two balanced involutions can use the same auxiliary columns with opposite body-shift directions, cancelling all body effects. For an odd correction, the balanced pair is followed by one transposition call; its sole residual effect is a cyclic permutation within one body, preserving that body's set. Each involution has at most q/2 pairs, so the total is O(q).
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Composition of the verified involution construction with the verified balanced factorization.

claims.claim: For arbitrary m,n≥2 and N=mn, any m×n configuration can be transformed in O(N log m) pushes into one in which every row contains exactly its target-row token set. In particular, this costs O(N log min{m,n}) when m≤n.
claims.evidence: After transposition and target-coordinate relabeling, original target rows are target columns of an n×m board. Claims 3–5 make every such column complete in O(N log m)+O(N)+O(m) pushes. Transposing back gives the original target-row sets. This reduction does not assume sortability and is valid for tall boards; only the logarithm remains log m there.
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Coordinate-by-coordinate transpose reduction, with each invoked primitive independently checked.

claims.claim: The parent's short-dimension reorientation does not justify its former row-specific O(N log min{m,n}) conclusion on a fixed tall labeling.
claims.evidence: On a tall board, reorientation exchanges row and column objectives: oriented-row membership maps back to original-column membership, not original-row membership. Thus the former inference is invalid even though the existential row-membership result is later recovered by another argument.
claims.witness: For the stated 3×2 output ((1,2),(5,4),(3,6)), the columns are {1,3,5} and {2,4,6}, while rows two and three are {4,5} and {3,6}, not {3,4} and {5,6}.
claims.search_method: Direct coordinate mapping and set comparison.

claims.claim: Assume 2≤m≤n and every row of a sortable m×n board already contains exactly its target-row token set. The board can then be sorted in O(mn) bidirectional pushes.
claims.evidence: Even row corrections use balanced involutions with cancelling side effects. If n is even, one row push changes the parity of an odd correction. If n is odd and m even, the residual transposition shifts an auxiliary body of odd length; that cycle is even and its inverse is implemented on the transposed board by two balanced involutions. If m,n are odd, sortability makes the number of odd rows even. Each is reduced to the same adjacent transposition, and paired rows are repaired by chained adjacent double swaps. The cost is O(mn+m²)=O(mn) because m≤n.
claims.witness: For adjacent rows r,r+1 and columns c,c+1, the eight-push word R_r^-1 C_c^-1 R_r C_c C_{c+1} R_{r+1} C_{c+1}^-1 R_{r+1}^-1 performs exactly the two required swaps. The checker verified this identity in 625 dimension/location cases.
claims.search_method: Complete parity-case proof plus exact permutation checks of all algebraic building blocks.

claims.claim: If min{m,n}=1 and N=mn, then D(m,n)=floor(N/2).
claims.evidence: All nonidentity moves reduce to the two directions of the unique length-N row or column. The reachable component is the cyclic group generated by one unit shift, whose distance for shift a is min(a mod N,N−a mod N). Its maximum is floor(N/2), including zero when N=1.
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Exact word metric of a cyclic group.

claims.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, and s=min{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·max{1,log s}); in particular, for m,n≥2, D(m,n)=O(N log s).
claims.evidence: For s≥2, transpose and relabel the entire sorting problem, if necessary, to an s×t board. Claim 6 supplies correct row sets in O(N log s), and Claim 8 completes sorting in O(N). This full-objective reorientation is a Cayley-graph isomorphism and does not repeat the row-specific error in Claim 7. Claim 9 handles s=1.
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Dependency audit of Claims 6, 8, and 9 with explicit coordinate reorientation.

claims.claim: For all m,n≥2, including tall boards, every configuration can in fact be transformed in O(N log min{m,n}) pushes into one with correct target-row token sets, but this is a corollary of the diameter bound rather than of the refuted transpose-back construction.
claims.evidence: If a dimension is even, every configuration is sortable and Claim 10 sorts it. On an odd-by-odd board, even configurations likewise sort. For an odd configuration A, choose B to be the sorted board with a within-row transposition. B is odd and already has correct row sets. Since A and B occupy the same A_N coset, vertex transitivity bounds their distance by the identity-component diameter from Claim 10. Claim 10 depends only on Claims 6 and 8, so this use is noncircular.
claims.witness: The comparison configuration B is the target board with any two tokens of one row exchanged.
claims.search_method: Cayley-coset and dependency-order proof.

claims.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
claims.evidence: With H and V the sums of shortest cyclic horizontal and vertical token displacements described in the sketch, one row push changes H by at most n and leaves V fixed; a column push has the symmetric property. The necessary row- and column-push counts therefore add. A global translation has H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), while shifting every row and column back along shortest directions attains the lower bound.
claims.witness: All translations on 2×2, 2×3, and 3×3 were checked against exact BFS distances.
claims.search_method: Lipschitz-potential proof and exhaustive exact-distance comparison.

claims.claim: The maximum possible value of the displacement certificate is exactly m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2), which is at most N; a half-translation attains it.
claims.evidence: Each of the N tokens contributes at most floor(n/2) to H and floor(m/2) to V. Since the resulting quotients are integers, the certificate is at most m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2)≤mn. Translating by the two half-period offsets makes every token attain both coordinate maxima simultaneously, proving equality.
claims.witness: The half-translation by (floor(n/2),floor(m/2)) attains the displayed value.
claims.search_method: Sharp coordinatewise upper bound and attaining construction; small boards exhaustively checked.

claims.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
claims.evidence: Claim 10 becomes O(N) when s is fixed. Claim 13 supplies a sortable half-translation with distance m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2)=Ω(N), with a positive constant for every fixed s≥2. The bounds match.
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Asymptotic combination of the verified upper bound and explicit translation lower bound.

claims.claim: A general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
claims.evidence: The reduced-word derivation is valid after adding m,n≥2, but the exact claim calls the bound general and supplies no such restriction after the draft has defined D on one-dimensional boards. For m=1,n=9, Claim 9 correctly gives D=4. The claimed substitutions give d=20 and Q=9!/2=181440, and 19^4=130321<1+18·181439/20<19^5, so the displayed ceiling is 5 and falsely asserts D≥5. The cause is that a 1×9 component has only nine cyclic shifts, not 9!/2 states.
claims.witness: m=1, n=9: actual D=4, claimed counting lower bound=5.
claims.search_method: Exact integer evaluation combined with the one-dimensional cyclic-group characterization.

claims.claim: The numerical counting certificate above is always at most 2N, so this reduced-word obstruction also cannot establish a superlinear lower bound.
claims.evidence: In the intended m,n≥2 domain, X=1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d<Q≤N!<N^N and d−1=2(m+n)−1>sqrt(N). Hence log_{d−1}X<2N, and its ceiling is at most the integer 2N. This numerical ceiling remains correct despite Claim 15's missing one-dimensional domain restriction.
claims.witness: The exact checker verified the ceiling for all 2≤m,n≤50.
claims.search_method: General logarithmic inequality with exact-integer grid checks.

claims.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
claims.evidence: Exact BFS using the seven distinct 2×3 generators visits all 720 configurations with levels [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], proving diameter 7. Claim 12 gives maximum translation distance 2·1+3·1=5.
claims.witness: The stated seven-push word reaches ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)); exact BFS places it at distance 7.
claims.search_method: Complete breadth-first enumeration and exact translation-distance calculation.

claims.claim: Exact square boundary cases give D(2,2)=4 and D(3,3)=8; on 3×3 the maximum displacement certificate is 6 and the counting certificate is 5.
claims.evidence: Complete BFS gives levels [1,4,10,8,1] on all 24 states of 2×2 and [1,12,96,736,5208,28674,89497,54741,2475] on all 181440 even states of 3×3, so the diameters are 4 and 8. The exact displacement formula gives 6 on 3×3, while direct integer evaluation of the reduced-word expression gives 5.
claims.witness: There are 2,475 configurations at distance 8 in the exact 3×3 enumeration.
claims.search_method: Complete Cayley-component BFS and exact integer certificate evaluation.

claims.claim: For growing s=min{m,n}, the established general bounds remain Ω(N)≤D(m,n)≤O(N log s), so the source target is not resolved at its requested strength.
claims.evidence: Half-translations give a uniform Ω(N) lower bound and Claim 10 gives O(N log s). When s is unbounded these differ by an unbounded logarithmic factor. Neither the displacement nor coarse counting certificate supplies that factor, and no O(N) general construction is proved, so asymptotically tight general bounds remain open.
claims.witness: none
claims.search_method: Target-coverage and asymptotic-gap audit.

target_evidence: The draft establishes material correct progress: O(N log min{m,n}) for all two-dimensional boards and Θ(N) whenever the shorter side is fixed. It nevertheless leaves Ω(N) versus O(N log s) when s grows, exactly the unresolved regime required by the source target. The overbroad one-dimensional wording of Claim 15 does not invalidate these central two-dimensional results, but it is a genuine refuted listed claim. The parent's PARTIAL label accurately describes target coverage.
checks_performed: Read only /evidence/source.json and /evidence/parent.json; used no web, retrieval database, receipt, other arm, prior-run evidence, or other solution.

The checker verified 4,720 SwapPairs instances, 5,913 permutation factorizations, 625 double-commutator identities, 1,467 FillColumns/FloatMinimums executions, all stated small-board BFS distributions, and the counting ceiling on 2,401 boards.
The checker reproduced the exact one-dimensional counterexample to Claim 15: on 1×9 the true diameter is 4 while its displayed expression evaluates to 5.
Independently audited the transpose dependencies, parity cases, Cayley-coset argument, displacement proof, asymptotic deductions, and target coverage.
